sessions.title: Grace That Offends and Judgment That Waits
sessions.aim: To hold together the parables of grace and of judgment, the vineyard workers who resent generosity, the unforgiving servant exposed by the mercy he received, and the sheep and goats surprised by their verdict, refusing both the sentiment that hears only grace and the moralism that hears only judgment.
sessions.summary:
The parables that trouble us most put grace and judgment in the same frame, and the trouble is the point. The question they press is whether we really want a God this generous, because grace landing on the wrong person can offend us as much as it comforts us.

In the vineyard, workers hired at different hours all receive a denarius, and the ones who worked all day are furious. They weren't cheated; the owner says, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?" (Matthew 20:13). Their complaint is that someone else got grace. Then the unforgiving servant, forgiven a debt he could never repay, who seizes a fellow servant over a hundred denarii. It's a mirror, and most of us are the first servant. Then the sheep and the goats, where both groups are surprised: the righteous didn't know they had served the King in "the least of these" (Matthew 25:40).

Judgment has been abused to frighten people, and the anger at that is often right. But a grace that judges nothing and costs nothing isn't grace. It's indifference. And in these stories judgment always falls on the one who received mercy and wouldn't pass it on. We aren't judged for failing to earn grace. We're judged for taking it and refusing to become people who give it.

keyScripture.why: "You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me. And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Matthew 18:32-33). The logic of all these parables is here: someone who has received a mercy beyond counting and refuses a small one hasn't understood what he received.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 20:1-15. The all-day workers weren't cheated, and they're still furious. Why does grace to someone else so often feel like an injustice against us?
discussion.behind: The all-day workers got exactly what they agreed to, and they still burn, because grace to another exposes the ledger in their own hearts. Help the room recognize the specific resentment: not at being wronged but at someone else receiving what they didn't earn.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 18:23-35. Where have you taken the mercy you received and refused to pass on a much smaller one?
discussion.behind: The parable only works when we see ourselves as the first servant. Go first with a real example. If someone names abuse or ongoing harm, don't treat it as a small debt; see the case study.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 25:31-46. Both groups are surprised. Why does it matter that the righteous didn't realize they were serving the King?
discussion.behind: The righteous weren't keeping score. They served the least of these, and the others assumed they'd have served the King if they'd seen him. Real obedience tends to be unselfconscious. The judgment falls on a love that calculated whom it was worth serving.

discussion.q: Some people say a God of judgment can't be a God of love. What's true in that, and what would we lose if we kept the grace and threw out the judgment?
discussion.behind: Honor the objector. Judgment used to frighten people is a real abuse. But a grace that cares nothing about what we do to each other isn't love. Help the room see that in these parables the judgment guards the seriousness of the grace.

discussion.q: In each of these stories, judgment falls on someone who received mercy and wouldn't extend it. How does that change the way you hear them?
discussion.behind: Let it land as both warning and invitation. We can't earn grace, and receiving it truly means being changed by it. End with the open question of whether the mercy we've received has made us merciful.

objections.objection: The vineyard parable is unfair. Paying someone who worked one hour the same as someone who worked twelve violates basic justice. People should be rewarded according to their effort.
objections.response: On the terms of justice the all-day workers have a case, and the parable doesn't pretend otherwise. The landowner speaks to it directly: "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?" (Matthew 20:13). Nobody was cheated. They got the full wage they agreed to. That's the hinge. Their grievance isn't that they were treated unjustly, because they weren't. It's that someone else was treated generously, and those are different complaints. The parable exposes a heart that can live with justice for itself but can't stand grace for another. The landowner's question cuts: "Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:15), or as the ESV notes it can be rendered, "is your eye bad because I am good?" The parable isn't defending unfairness. It asks why God's goodness to people we think undeserving fills us with resentment. We wanted a God who pays by the ledger, and we got a God who gives.

objections.objection: The sheep and goats parable makes salvation about works: feeding the hungry, visiting the prisoner. That contradicts grace and turns the gospel into a checklist that earns heaven.
objections.response: Grace isn't earned, and a reading that turns the gospel into a scored checklist has lost the center. But look at what distinguishes the sheep from the goats. It isn't a tally. It's surprise. "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink?" (Matthew 25:37). The righteous had no idea they'd served the King. Their mercy wasn't performed for a reward or logged toward a total; it was what they'd become. That's the opposite of works-righteousness, which keeps exactly the score the sheep didn't keep. The parable isn't teaching that you earn heaven by deeds. It's teaching that a heart changed by grace becomes merciful without noticing, and that the absence of any mercy at all shows a heart grace never reached. The fruit isn't the price of grace. It's the sign that grace was real.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where have you taken the mercy God gave you and quietly refused to become someone who gives it, keeping a ledger against a person who owes you far less than you were forgiven?
sessions.practice: This week, find the fellow servant you've been holding by the throat, the person you keep a small debt against while you've been forgiven an enormous one. Let it go in prayer, and in person if it's wise and safe. If what was done to you is abuse or still dangerous, letting go of the debt never means going back within reach; talk to the leader about getting help. Then look for one of "the least of these" you've been passing without seeing, and serve them without counting it. Write down where the mercy you received has and hasn't yet made you merciful.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you forgave us a debt we couldn't have counted, let alone paid, and then you watched us walk out of that mercy and take a brother by the throat over what he owed us. Forgive us for taking your grace and refusing to give it. Forgive the ledgers we keep against people you've already forgiven, and the resentment we feel when your generosity lands on someone we judged undeserving. Break the accounting in us. Make us like the sheep who served you without knowing it, so changed by your mercy that we give it away without noticing. And where we haven't become that yet, don't let us mistake your grace for a grace that leaves us unchanged. Amen.
reflection: When God is generous to someone I think hasn't earned it, do I rejoice or resent, and what does that say about the ledger in my heart?
Where am I the unforgiving servant, forgiven a debt beyond counting and still collecting a small one?
Has the mercy I received made me merciful toward the least of these, or have I taken the grace and stayed the same?
sessions.teaching:
The parables that trouble us most are the ones that won't separate grace from judgment, that put both in the same frame and won't let us keep one and throw out the other. The trouble they cause isn't a flaw. It's their work.

Start with the vineyard, because it shows something in us we'd rather not see. A landowner goes out early and hires workers for a denarius, a standard day's wage, a fair deal freely agreed. He goes out again at nine, at noon, at three, and at five, an hour before quitting time, and hires more, promising the later ones only "whatever is right" (Matthew 20:4). At evening he pays them all a denarius, starting with the last, so the all-day workers watch it happen. They're furious. "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat" (Matthew 20:12). Feel the exact shape of that anger. They weren't cheated. The owner says so: "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?" (Matthew 20:13). Their complaint isn't that justice was denied them. It's that grace was given to someone else. Then the question aimed at us: "Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:15). We all believe we love grace, right up until it's given to someone we think should have had to earn it.

Then the unforgiving servant, which may be the most searching parable in the Gospels, because it's built as a mirror. A servant owes his king ten thousand talents, a sum meant to sound impossible, more than anyone could earn in many lifetimes. "And out of pity for him, the master of that servant released him and forgave him the debt" (Matthew 18:27). The servant walks straight out of that mercy, finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, a real debt of about a hundred days' wages, "and seizing him, he began to choke him, saying, 'Pay what you owe'" (Matthew 18:28). We recoil from him, and the recoil is the trap, because we're the first servant. We've been forgiven a debt against God we couldn't begin to count, and then we go out and collect: the slight, the thing they said, the way they wronged us. I know the feeling of the grip tightening on someone else's throat while the size of what was cancelled for me fades from memory.

I need to add a careful word. A real wrong done to you, especially abuse, isn't trivial, and this parable doesn't ask you to pretend it is or to put yourself back within reach of harm. Forgiving is letting go of the right to make someone pay. It isn't excusing what they did or trusting them again.

Then the sheep and the goats, where the surprise is the thing to see. The King says to those on his right, "I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35). And they don't know what he's talking about. "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you?" (Matthew 25:37). They'd served the hungry and the stranger and the prisoner without calculating, without any notion they were building a case. "Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40). The others are surprised too, from the other side. They'd happily have served a visible King. It never occurred to them he was hidden in the people they walked past.

Now the strongest objection: a God of judgment can't be a God of love. The anger behind that is often right. Judgment has been used to frighten and control, preached by people who used hell as a weapon, and recoiling from that can be closer to defending God than rejecting him. Grant it. But take judgment out of these parables entirely and you don't get a more loving God. You get an indifferent one. A grace that judges nothing and cares nothing about what we do to each other isn't grace at all. It's a shrug dressed up as love, a God who watches the forgiven servant choke his neighbor and feels nothing. The judgment in these stories is the seriousness of the grace, the sign that the mercy was real enough to matter.

And look at whom the judgment falls on in every case. Not on someone who failed to earn grace; no one earns it. It falls on the one who received mercy and refused to extend it. The worker who got his fair wage and resented grace to another. The servant forgiven everything who collected his small debt anyway. The goats who received their very lives from God and had no mercy for the least of these. We aren't judged for failing to earn grace. We're judged for taking it and refusing to become people who give it away. That leaves the weight where these parables mean to leave it, on a question we have to carry home. The debt has been cancelled, all ten thousand talents. Has the mercy we received made us merciful, or did we take the whole fortune and walk out looking for someone who owed us a hundred denarii?

scriptureStudy.note: "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?... Or do you begrudge my generosity?" Justice was fully met. The workers' grievance is resentment of grace to another.

"One was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents... And out of pity for him, the master of that servant released him and forgave him the debt." The sum is meant to be beyond repaying, so the mercy is total.
"But when that same servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii, and seizing him, he began to choke him." The gap between the two debts is the mirror.
"Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" Received mercy calls for extended mercy, and refusing it shows the mercy was never grasped.
"Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you?... As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me." The righteous are surprised; their mercy wasn't calculated.

"Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?" The others would have served a visible King and missed him hidden in the least of these.
"Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful." The Father's mercy is both the measure and the source of the mercy we owe.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how these parables have been read in two opposite wrong directions. One reading keeps only the comfort and softens the judgment into a warning with no weight. Klyne Snodgrass's Stories with Intent insists the parables of judgment be read in their first-century setting and not softened. The other reading turns the sheep and goats into a checklist of deeds and loses grace entirely. Notice that the parable's own emphasis on surprise cuts against any scoring of deeds.

Then set this beside the long argument over grace and works that the Reformation fought. These parables refuse a false choice. We're saved by a grace we can't earn, and that grace, if it's real, produces mercy, as the unforgiving servant shows by its absence. Finally, take the pastoral turn. Our culture prefers a God who affirms and never judges, and much of the church has gone along, offering a grace so cheap it asks nothing and changes no one. These parables hold that mercy is free and also makes a total claim: forgiven ten thousand talents, we're no longer free to collect our hundred denarii. Ask the group whether they've traded the offense of these stories for a comfortable grace that leaves the ledger untouched.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is carrying a grievance, and it surfaces at the unforgiving servant. Someone has genuinely wronged him, a betrayal or a debt or a real injury. He says, with some heat, that forgiveness can't mean pretending it didn't happen or letting the person off with no consequences, and that people who preach easy forgiveness have never been hurt the way he has.

He's right that the wound is real, so honor it. The parable doesn't make the hundred denarii imaginary; it's a real debt, and cheap forgiveness that ignores harm is its own failure. Then help him see what the parable actually asks: not that he pretend the wound was nothing, but that he weigh it against what he himself has been forgiven, and ask whether he's holding his brother by the throat.

Where the wound is grave, where there has been abuse or harm is still going on, make the distinction plain. Forgiving the debt isn't returning to danger, and the parable doesn't require that. Make sure he knows how to find real help, including the Find Help page on this site, and offer to talk privately. Then ask the group where the mercy they've received has begun, or not yet begun, to loosen their grip on what they're owed.

memoryVerse.text: And the King will answer them, Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a study on the parables is that everyone already knows the stories, and knowing them is exactly what keeps people from being caught by them. A group can spend five weeks admiring the parables from a safe distance, nodding at the running father and the good Samaritan and the mustard seed, retrieving the lesson each was filed under years ago, and never once standing where the story means to leave them. A room like that isn't being formed. It's being confirmed.

So set one rule the first night and keep it. The useful question is rarely "what does this parable teach?", which lets you hold it at arm's length. It's "where am I standing in it?" Push the room, gently and steadily, past the moral and into the mirror. When you reach the older brother, don't let the room locate him in absent Pharisees; the parable was aimed at religious people, and this is a room of religious people. When you reach the good Samaritan, don't let it stay a lesson in kindness; ask people to name the person they'd least want cast as the hero. When you reach the unforgiving servant, go first and name your own hundred denarii. The parables do their deepest work in the silence after recognition, so make room for that silence instead of rushing to an application.

Guard against two opposite failures. Some will want to reduce every parable to a simple moral so they never have to be undone by it, and some will want to decode every detail into a hidden doctrine. Both are ways of controlling a story built to control you. Keep bringing the room back to the single sharp edge of each one.

Session 5 touches forgiveness, and someone in the room may be carrying a real injury, even abuse. Don't press forgiveness on the wounded. Make the distinction clear: letting go of the right to make someone pay is never the same as going back within reach of harm. Know where the Find Help page on this site is, and a pastor or counselor you can refer someone to, before you begin.

Lead from inside the stories, not above them. If you present yourself as the one who has these stories mastered, the room will admire them with you and none of you will be caught. Go in as a hearer still finding yourself in the character you didn't want to be. Five weeks won't exhaust the parables. They can teach a room to hear them again as Jesus built them, gentle traps for the conscience that leave a person standing where they didn't mean to stand.

faq.q: Did Jesus really tell parables to hide the truth, or is that a misreading of Mark 4?
faq.a: He said it plainly: "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables" (Mark 4:11), and he quoted Isaiah 6. The parable isn't only a teaching aid; it reveals and conceals at once. But be careful about what the concealing means. In Mark 4 the explanation goes to those who come near and ask (Mark 4:34), so the difference isn't a locked door but nearness and hunger. The parable withholds itself from the person who has already decided what it's allowed to mean, and that keeps it from being reduced to a slogan he can master and walk away from.

faq.q: Why is it called the prodigal son if the study says it's about two sons?
faq.a: The traditional title fixes our eyes on the younger son, and that makes it easy to miss the second half, which was aimed at the people Jesus was talking to. Luke 15 opens with the Pharisees grumbling that Jesus "receives sinners and eats with them." The parable answers that grumble, first with the younger son who rebels and is welcomed, then with the older son who never left and is just as lost, angry at the grace shown to his brother. The father goes out to both. The story ends without telling us whether the older brother came in, because the grumblers were standing on the same threshold.

faq.q: Is the good Samaritan just about being kind to people in need?
faq.a: The plain lesson is real: help the person bleeding in the ditch. But calling it simply a lesson in kindness is how we defuse it. The lawyer, "desiring to justify himself," asks "who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29), a request for a boundary. Jesus makes the hero a Samaritan, an enemy and a heretic to the lawyer, and then doesn't answer the question. He asks which of the three "proved to be a neighbor," turning a category into something you do. The parable goes straight at the boundaries we draw around the love we owe.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a session on small parables like the mustard seed and the leaven?
faq.a: Because together they make an argument the church needs and our culture resists: the kingdom of God arrives in ways too small and hidden to impress. The crowds wanted a throne and an army, and Jesus gave them a mustard seed, leaven hidden in dough, and treasure buried in a field. The smallness isn't the kingdom's weakness; it's the method. We're formed by a world that equates significance with size, and these parables insist that God works through what the world overlooks, the "day of small things" (Zechariah 4:10).

faq.q: Does the sheep and goats parable mean we're saved by good works?
faq.a: No. What distinguishes the sheep from the goats isn't a tally of deeds but surprise. The righteous had no idea they'd served the King: "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you?" (Matthew 25:37). Their mercy wasn't logged toward a total; it was the overflow of a heart changed by grace. That's the opposite of earning, which keeps the score the sheep didn't keep. The parable teaches that a heart changed by grace becomes merciful without noticing, and that a total absence of mercy shows a heart grace never reached. The fruit isn't the price of grace. It's the evidence that grace was real.

faq.q: The vineyard parable seems unfair. Is God really fine with paying people the same for unequal work?
faq.a: On the terms of justice the all-day workers have a case, and the landowner speaks to it: "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?" (Matthew 20:13). Nobody was cheated. Their complaint is that someone else was treated generously. The parable exposes a heart that can live with justice for itself but can't stand grace for another. "Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:15). It isn't defending unfairness. It's asking why God's goodness to people we think undeserving makes us resentful.

faq.q: How can a God of judgment also be a God of love? The judgment parables trouble me.
faq.a: That trouble deserves respect. Judgment has been used to frighten and control people, and recoiling from that is often closer to defending God than rejecting him. But if you take the judgment out of these parables and keep only the grace, you don't get a more loving God; you get an indifferent one who doesn't care what we do to each other. The judgment is the seriousness of the grace. And notice where it falls: not on those who failed to earn grace, since no one does, but on those who received mercy and refused to extend it.

faq.q: Why does the study keep saying the parables are meant to catch us rather than just teach us?
faq.a: Because that's how Jesus built them. A parable lets you judge the story before you realize the story is judging you, the way Nathan told David about a stolen lamb and David condemned the man before Nathan said, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). Tell a proud man he's proud and he defends himself. Tell him a story and let him pronounce the verdict, and then hand him the mirror. So the study keeps asking not only what a parable teaches but where we're standing in it.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Aren't the parables just moral folklore dressed up as revelation?
faq.a: It's a fair question, and the study tries not to overclaim. At one level the parables are some of the most arresting short stories ever told, and their moral power is real whatever you think of their teller. But notice how they behave. They don't reassure the way folklore usually does. They make the enemy the hero, leave the respectable man outside the party, and refuse to resolve. Folklore tends to comfort the tribe; these stories were built to catch the very people listening. Try reading one slowly, as if for the first time, and see whether it only confirms a moral you already hold or finds you standing somewhere you didn't mean to stand. You don't have to believe anything to try that.

faq.q: Some of these parables are hard, even frightening. Should we really study them in a small group?
faq.a: Yes, and carefully. Every question carries notes for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than in the anxiety hard parables can stir. The parables of judgment are meant to be taken seriously; Jesus spoke of judgment often. But the study never lets judgment stand alone. It shows that judgment falls on the refusal of a mercy freely given, so the hard parables are finally about the seriousness of grace. Handled that way, they leave a group sobered and, underneath, freed: the debt has been cancelled, and the remaining question is whether that mercy has made us merciful. If anyone is carrying a wound that the forgiveness session touches, the leader will make sure they know where to find help.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm not a Bible scholar and don't know the background?
faq.a: That's the design. The study was written to be led by ordinary people. Each discussion question carries notes, and the background you need, drawn from scholars like Kenneth Bailey and Klyne Snodgrass, is in the sessions where you need it. The real qualification isn't scholarship but willingness to go first: to say where you find yourself in the older brother or the unforgiving servant, and to keep the room from admiring the parables at a distance. Read the leader primer, sit with the story yourself before the meeting, and go first.

timeline.event: The prophet Nathan confronts King David with a story about a rich man who takes a poor man's only lamb, and David condemns the man before Nathan says, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12).
Isaiah receives the commission of Isaiah 6, to preach to a people whose ears will stay heavy, the passage Jesus quotes to explain why he speaks in parables.
Jesus teaches in Galilee, often in parables: the sower, the mustard seed, the leaven, announcing a kingdom too small and hidden to satisfy those waiting for a throne and an army.

On the way to Jerusalem and in his last days there, Jesus tells the parables Luke and Matthew preserve: the good Samaritan, the two lost sons, the vineyard workers, the unforgiving servant, and the sheep and the goats.
The Gospel writers gather and arrange the parables: Mark clusters the kingdom parables in chapter 4, Matthew in chapter 13, and Luke preserves parables of grace found nowhere else.

Augustine reads the good Samaritan as an allegory, with the wounded man as Adam, the inn as the church, and the two coins as the two commandments of love, a way of reading that ran for more than a thousand years.
Adolf Jülicher publishes his two-volume work on the parables, reacting against allegory by insisting each parable makes one main point, a correction that also flattened some of their sharpness.
C. H. Dodd publishes The Parables of the Kingdom, arguing that the parables announce a kingdom already arriving in Jesus' ministry.
Joachim Jeremias publishes The Parables of Jesus, seeking their original setting in Jesus' ministry, often read as moving Dodd toward a kingdom already present and still to come.
Kenneth Bailey publishes The Cross and the Prodigal, the first of several books drawing on his years in the Middle East to recover the cultural shock of the parables.
Klyne Snodgrass publishes Stories with Intent, a comprehensive study reading the parables in their first-century setting and resisting both allegory and the softening of the parables of judgment.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. Before we start, three things. First, almost everyone here already knows these stories, and knowing them can keep us from being caught by them. We're not here to review the parables. We're here to stand inside them. Second, the question we'll keep coming back to isn't only what a parable teaches, but where each of us is standing in it, and we'll keep asking it even when it's uncomfortable. Third, I'm not up here as someone who has these stories figured out. I find myself in the older brother and the priest crossing the road as often as anyone. What's said here stays here. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this parable says. Now let's bring it off the page and into the week each of us came in from, because none of this matters if it stays a lesson about the parable and never becomes the mirror it was built to be.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't resolved. The parables don't tie a bow on things, and Jesus left more than one of these stories open on purpose, waiting to see where the hearer would stand. Take this home with you. Try the practice this week, sit with the reflection questions, and let the parable keep looking at you. Come back ready to be candid, not finished. I'll pray for us before we go, and my door is open if any of you needs it.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree to stand inside the stories rather than only explain them, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Why He Spoke in Riddles, full discussion and practice, with extended time on Mark 4 and Isaiah 6.
Week 3: Session 2, Two Lost Sons and a Father Who Runs, part one, the younger son and the running father and the scandal Bailey recovers.
Week 4: Session 2 continued: the older brother and the open ending, with time on where the room finds itself in the field.
Week 5: Session 3, The Question That Traps the Man Who Asks It, naming the actual enemy each person would least want cast as the hero.
Week 6: Session 4, The Kingdom Comes Small, the mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, and the sower, with time on measuring by harvest rather than waste.
Week 7: Session 5, Grace That Offends and Judgment That Waits, holding grace and judgment together, with care for anyone carrying a real injury.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and the character each person kept finding themselves in, closing in the mercy that makes us merciful.

Week 2: Session 3, The Question That Traps the Man Who Asks It, with time to name the real enemy the parable casts as hero.
Week 3: Session 4, The Kingdom Comes Small, the kingdom parables and the method of smallness.
Week 4: Session 5, Grace That Offends and Judgment That Waits, plus a short integration close in the mercy that makes us merciful.

bibliography.author: Craig L. Blomberg
bibliography.note: Blomberg (1990; 2nd ed. 2012) defends a reading in which a parable may carry more than one point without collapsing into allegory. Background on interpretation across the study.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Luke
bibliography.author: Luke
bibliography.note: Preserves the prodigal son and the good Samaritan, found in no other Gospel. The primary text for sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Matthew
bibliography.author: Matthew
bibliography.note: Gathers the kingdom parables in chapter 13 and the vineyard, the unforgiving servant, and the sheep and the goats. The primary text for sessions 4 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Mark
bibliography.author: Mark
bibliography.note: Clusters the kingdom parables in chapter 4 and keeps Jesus' explanation of why he teaches in parables. The primary text for session 1.

furtherReading: The Prodigal God, Timothy Keller, for groups who want the fuller pastoral case behind session 2's reading of two lost sons.
Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, Kenneth Bailey, for the cultural background behind the prodigal, the Samaritan and much else.
Stories with Intent, Klyne Snodgrass, for a thorough modern guide to the parables in their first-century setting.
The Parables of the Kingdom, C. H. Dodd, for the argument that the kingdom was already arriving in Jesus; background for sessions 1 and 4.
Luke 15 and Matthew 25, read straight through, to let the parables of grace and of judgment speak without a commentary in the way.

glossary.definition: A short story drawn from common life, in C. H. Dodd's words "arresting the hearer by its vividness or strangeness," and open enough to tease the mind into thought. Built less to settle a lesson than to get past the guard a direct command would trip.

The double work of the parable named in Mark 4: it shows the kingdom to those who come near and ask, and stays a riddle to those who have already decided what it may mean, so the same story opens one heart and hardens another.
The sower's image for the heart that receives the word: path, rock, thorns or good ground. The seed is the same everywhere; what it yields depends on the ground.
The study's reading of Luke 15: two lost sons, not one. The younger is lost in rebellion, the older inside his obedience, and the father goes out to both.

The scandal at the center of Luke 15, as Kenneth Bailey reads it: a man of standing giving up his dignity to run to a son who had wished him dead, taking on himself the shame the village would have put on the boy.
The lawyer's question in Luke 10, which Luke says he asked "desiring to justify himself": a request for a boundary around the obligation to love, the instinct the good Samaritan takes apart.
God's reign, announced in the parables as already arriving in Jesus, not with a throne and an army but like a mustard seed and hidden leaven. Its smallness is its method.
C. H. Dodd's term for the claim that the kingdom of God was already present in Jesus' ministry rather than only predicted, later held by many as a kingdom already begun and not yet complete.
The parable of Matthew 18, a mirror in which the hearer is the servant forgiven a debt beyond counting who then chokes a fellow servant over a hundred denarii.
What the vineyard parable exposes: grace to someone we judge undeserving can offend us as much as it comforts us, because to a heart keeping a ledger, another's undeserved blessing feels like theft.
The parables' refusal to separate the two. A grace that judges nothing isn't grace but indifference, and the judgment falls on the one who received mercy and wouldn't extend it.
The phrase from Matthew 25 for the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the imprisoned, in whom the King is hidden, so that mercy shown to them is shown to him.
Reading every detail of a parable as a code for a hidden doctrine, as when the Samaritan's inn becomes the church. It ran for more than a thousand years and often buried each story's single edge.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Most of us have heard the parables so many times we've stopped hearing them. This five-session study walks back into the stories Jesus built not only to teach us but to catch us: why he spoke in parables at all; the two lost sons of Luke 15 and the father who runs; the good Samaritan and the question a lawyer used to protect himself; the kingdom parables and the strange smallness of how God works; and the parables of grace and judgment that offend us and search us. Drawing on Kenneth Bailey, C. H. Dodd and Klyne Snodgrass, it recovers the shock the first hearers couldn't miss. Any group can lead it with little preparation. Come to be caught, not confirmed.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on the parables of Jesus, and if you think you already know these stories, that's exactly the point. We know them so well we've stopped being caught by them, and Jesus built them to catch. This study walks back into the prodigal son, the good Samaritan, the mustard seed, the unforgiving servant and more, and recovers the shock the first hearers felt. It won't just teach you the lesson. It aims to leave you standing where you didn't mean to stand. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Most of us have heard the parables so often we no longer hear them. Five sessions on the stories Jesus built to catch us: why he spoke in riddles, the two lost sons and the father who runs, the Samaritan and the lawyer's question, the kingdom that comes small, and the grace that offends and the judgment that waits. Come to be caught, not confirmed.
quoteCards: Jesus didn't tell riddles to keep people out. He told them to get in.
A parable lets you judge the story before you understand that the story is judging you.
There are two lost sons in Luke 15, and one of them never left home.
A man of standing didn't run. This father ran to reach his son before the village could.
The lawyer wanted a noun to define. Jesus gave him a verb to do.
The smallness isn't the kingdom's weakness. It's the method.
Most of us are the first servant: forgiven everything, and still collecting.
We aren't judged for failing to earn grace. We're judged for refusing to become people who give it.
